title: Naval Topic 3 生词 · 单词卡

cards.ex: An insight is a clear, deep understanding of something, often a surprising one. Chris says one of your insights to mean one of Naval's smart ideas. We often say gain insight into something.
exs: That book gave me real insight into how money works.
Thanks, that's a great insight.

cards.ex: To quip means to say something short, clever and a little funny. I quipped that means Naval once said it as a witty line. Quipped is the past tense.
exs: "At least the coffee's good," she quipped.
He's always ready with a quick quip.

cards.ex: Hopefully means I hope this happens. Here: you win the games, and then, if all goes well, you get bored of them. It's one of the most common words in spoken American English.
exs: Hopefully the traffic won't be bad.
I'll finish early today, hopefully.

cards.ex: Bored means you've lost interest and feel there's nothing exciting. Get bored of something means you've done it enough and don't care anymore. Bored with is also common.
exs: I got bored of that show after two episodes.
Kids get bored so fast on long drives.

cards.ex: To loop means to go around and around and repeat. Keep looping on the same game means playing the same game again and again without moving on. It's also used for songs and videos that repeat.
exs: This song has been looping in my head all day.
Set the video to loop.

cards.ex: Although connects two ideas that seem to go against each other. Naval says don't keep looping, although these games are very enticing. It means the same as even though, and sounds a bit more formal than but.
exs: Although I was tired, I went to the gym.
I liked the movie, although it was a little long.

cards.ex: Enticing means very attractive in a way that pulls you in and makes you want it. Naval means these games are tempting, so it's hard to stop. Often used for food, offers and ideas.
exs: That dessert looks really enticing.
They made me an enticing job offer.

cards.ex: Relatively means compared to other things, not in an absolute way. Relatively open-ended means the games don't really have a clear end, compared to most games. Americans use it all the time to soften a statement.
exs: The test was relatively easy.
It's a relatively new salon, but it's already busy.

cards.ex: Either … or gives you two choices, and usually you pick one. Naval says either you move to a different game or you play just for joy. In speech, either often comes first to set up the choice.
exs: We can either eat in or go out.
Either you call her or I will.

cards.ex: Sheer means pure and nothing else, and it makes a feeling or amount sound very strong. For the sheer joy of it means only because it's fun, with no other goal. We also say sheer luck or sheer size.
exs: She dances for the sheer joy of it.
We won by sheer luck.
